Table~\ref{tab:pairwise_significance} reports pairwise paired $t$-test results for the 6 main filtering strategies ($\binom{6}{2} = 15$ comparisons), with Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction: raw $p$-values are sorted ascending, each multiplied by its remaining-hypotheses count ($m - \text{rank} + 1$), and the cumulative maximum is applied to enforce monotonicity.

\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{sec:extended_discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations---establishes that this boundary is remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B scale.

The shallowness is explained by the rate of information loss.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$), reflecting the large distributional gap between human and first-generation text.
At 1v2, $\auc$ drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp (range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all conditions), indicating that the majority of discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By 2v3, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.

This pattern aligns with model collapse findings.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating predictable tail probability mass loss.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that operationally, this approach is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

The consistency across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy, nucleus ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ in $[0.6866, 0.7039]$.
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength but does not shift the boundary, suggesting that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the information bottleneck of the generation process rather than sampling algorithm properties.

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer Implications}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that the relative importance of depth features is largely text-intrinsic: feature rankings are highly correlated across scorers ($\rho > 0.90$), and cross-model classification retains 80--92\% accuracy (Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo: 90--92\%; broader continuation-mode pairs: 80--92\%).
However, absolute discriminability at the $\Kempirical$ boundary is scorer-sensitive---alternative scorers reduce Qwen-continuation $\Kempirical$ from 2 to 1, while rewrite-mode $\Kempirical = 2$ is preserved (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
At 0v1, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 for all pairs, confirming fully transferable binary contamination detection.

A single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed for texts from other models without retraining---extending utility to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown.

Two caveats: (1)~a nontrivial model-specific residual persists despite high transfer, and (2)~Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cross-scorer validation on Qwen-generated text. Alternative scorers (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B) preserve feature ranking ($\rho > 0.90$) and rewrite-mode $\Kempirical = 2$, but reduce continuation-mode $\Kempirical$ from 2 to 1. $\dagger$: CI lower bound below $\theta{=}0.60$. Underlined: $\auc < \theta$.}
\label{tab:crossscorer}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/tab_crossscorer}}
\end{table}

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is consistent across decoding strategies, feature importance ordering varies.
Greedy and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with vocabulary diversity measures dominating.
Greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction).
$T{=}1.2$ promotes \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to top ranks; \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 (greedy) to rank~5.

The \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} depends on sampling strategy.
A general-purpose classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups.

\subsection{Scale Considerations}

Our $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\leq$1.5B constitutes a methodological lower bound.
All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics without model internals, and cross-model transfer (80--92\%) demonstrates methodology generalization across architectures.

Scaling to larger models presents two outcomes: if $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ (as scaling laws suggest~\cite{dohmatob2024model}), depth contamination becomes more insidious and our framework more necessary; if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists, our conclusions generalize directly.
The high cross-model transfer across three architecturally distinct families provides indirect evidence that depth signals are not tied to a specific pretraining paradigm.

\subsection{Cross-Model Neural Probe Analysis}
\label{sec:extended_neural_probe}

The neural probe (frozen-encoder MLP on each model's own hidden states) yields model-dependent $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}}$: Qwen-continuation achieves 2v3 $\auc = 0.6159$ $[0.610, 0.622]$, exceeding $\theta$ for $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$; Pythia-1.4B ($\auc_{2v3} = 0.5963$ $[0.589, 0.603]$) and OLMo-1B ($\auc_{2v3} = 0.5892$ $[0.582, 0.597]$) both fall below $\theta$, matching the 15D boundary at $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 2$.

The Qwen-only elevation is consistent with a \emph{self-familiarity} effect: each probe uses the generator's own frozen embeddings to classify its own outputs.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, as an instruction-tuned model, encodes richer mode-specific artifacts in its hidden states that enable finer depth discrimination---but these artifacts do not transfer across model families.
By contrast, the 15D hand-crafted features yield $\Kempirical = 2$ universally across all three models, confirming that model-free statistical features provide a more robust and transferable depth signal.

This result strengthens the practical case for model-free features: $\Ktheory \geq 3$ can only be claimed for Qwen representations specifically, while the model-free $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary holds as a feature-set-specific lower bound across all tested architectures.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:extended_llm}

On a balanced 500-sample test set (5 depth classes, 100 per depth), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% (MAE = 1.15)---comparable to OBD-LightGBM's 38.0\% (95\% CI: $[0.340, 0.422]$) on the same subset (Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
McNemar exact tests confirm that the OBD--LLM accuracy differences are not statistically significant ($p = 0.081$ vs.\ GPT-5.5, $p = 0.069$ vs.\ Claude); bootstrap 95\% CIs for the accuracy difference include or border zero ($[-0.4, +10.0]$\,pp vs.\ GPT-5.5; $[0.0, +10.2]$\,pp vs.\ Claude).
Both LLMs achieve ${\sim}$88\% binary accuracy.

The per-depth breakdown reveals where OBD's nominal $+$4.8\,pp gap originates and, more importantly, where \emph{all} methods fail.
OBD per-depth recall: depth-0 96\%, depth-1 39\%, depth-2 14\%, depth-3 19\%, depth-4 22\%.
GPT-5.5 recall: 77\% (depth-0), 8--38\% (depths 2--4); Claude: 69\% (depth-0), 10--37\% (depths 2--4).
OBD's advantage derives entirely from depth-0 identification; for depths 2--4, OBD recall collapses to 14--22\%---comparable to or below LLM recall.
This convergent failure across fundamentally different approaches---supervised statistical classification and zero-shot frontier LLMs---confirms that the $\Kempirical = 2$ saturation is a property of the data rather than a method limitation.
Fine-grained depth discrimination beyond depth~1 fails regardless of whether the classifier is trained on depth labels or prompted with chain-of-thought reasoning.

Spearman correlations between true and predicted depth are weak for all methods ($\rho = 0.38$--$0.42$ for LLMs), confirming that generational depth estimation beyond the binary boundary remains an open challenge.
Statistical detection methods (DetectGPT~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt}, Binoculars~\cite{hans2024binoculars}) optimize scalar scores for the binary boundary---the same distinction where all approaches succeed.

\paragraph{Sensitivity to probability merging.}
When 6-class OBD probabilities are marginalized to 5 classes by merging $P(d{=}4)+P(d{=}5) \to P(d{\geq}4)$, accuracy rises to 44.4\% (McNemar $p < 0.001$ vs.\ LLMs), but the gain concentrates in depth-4 (recall: 22\%$\to$80\%) while depths 2--3 collapse to 2--8\%.
The raw 6-class evaluation (38.0\%) avoids this single-class bias and is reported as the primary result.

\subsection{Broader Impact}

The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled text---a one-wash laundering effect that limits filtering granularity.

$\Kstar$ provides a corpus audit metric: what fraction of a training corpus consists of depth-$\geq 2$ text?
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic without expensive retraining experiments.

\subsection{Degradation and Practical Considerations}

In our continual training experiments (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}), all strategies degrade the base model's general capabilities (MMLU: 0.6018 $\to$ 0.5865--0.5941; HellaSwag: 0.6821 $\to$ 0.6638--0.6701).
This must be interpreted in context: our 100\% synthetic setting provides an upper-bound characterization.
In realistic mixed-corpus settings, degradation is proportional to the contamination fraction~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
Even under this extreme condition, $\Kstar$-aware binary filtering reduces MMLU degradation from $-$1.53\,pp to $-$0.77\,pp---an approximately 50\% reduction.

Binary filtering at the $\Kstar = 2$ boundary requires no per-model calibration, is simple to implement, and is universally applicable across tested generator configurations.
Combining depth-aware filtering with distribution-matching methods (DSIR, DoReMi) is a promising direction.

\subsection{Extended Limitations}
\label{sec:extended_limitations}

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our prompt-chain protocol holds model quality constant; real-world retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics.
Under the monotonic-degradation assumption~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}, $\Kstar^{\text{retrain}} \leq \Kstar^{\text{prompt}}$, making our $\Kempirical = 2$ a conservative estimate.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
All $\Kempirical$ values below use the 95\% CI lower bound criterion (Eq.~\ref{eq:kstar}).
At $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 3$ for Qwen-rewrite and Qwen-continuation (2v3 CI lower bounds 0.5795 and 0.5511), while Pythia and OLMo remain at $\Kempirical = 2$ (2v3 CI lower bounds 0.5417 and 0.5399).
At $\theta = 0.65$, all three continuation-mode configurations drop to $\Kempirical = 1$ (1v2 CI lower bounds: Pythia 0.6454, OLMo 0.6045, Qwen-continuation 0.6015) while Qwen-rewrite retains $\Kempirical = 2$ (1v2 CI lower bound 0.6859).
At $\theta = 0.70$, $\Kempirical = 1$ universally.
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant (Figure~\ref{fig:kstar_theta}).

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.15\,pp; Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by 0.09\,pp.
All eight boundary comparisons yield permutation $p < 0.01$.

\emph{Graduated filtering.}
Graduated filtering at all tested $\alpha$ values (0.1--0.9) underperforms binary-ours on MMLU (best: $0.5892$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$ vs.\ $0.5941$), with a monotonic trend.
At $\alpha{=}0.9$, HellaSwag matches binary-ours exactly ($0.6701$), consistent with $\Kempirical = 2$ predicting no benefit from finer ordinal structure.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Why $\Kempirical = 2$: The Information Bottleneck}
\label{sec:why_kstar}

The shallowness of $\Kempirical = 2$ is explained by the concentration of information loss in the first generation step.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$): autoregressive generation systematically compresses the heavy-tailed, bursty surprisal patterns characteristic of human language, even in a single pass.
At 1v2, $\auc$ drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp (range: 0.6112--0.7039), indicating that the majority of the remaining discriminative signal is consumed in one additional step.
By 2v3, $\auc$ falls below $\theta$ (0.5496--0.5917), and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
This rapid convergence reflects the generation operator acting as a lossy channel with diminishing marginal information loss: the first pass removes the most distinguishing structure, and subsequent passes operate on already-smoothed distributions.
The consistency of $\Kempirical = 2$ across four decoding strategies (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}) reinforces this interpretation---higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength but does not shift the boundary, confirming that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation process itself rather than the sampling algorithm.
Even at the most marginal condition (Qwen-continuation, where the 95\% CI lower bound exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.15\,pp), $\Kempirical = 2$ survives under self-scoring---suggesting that the boundary is genuine rather than an artifact of generous thresholding.

Per-depth analysis provides the most direct evidence that this boundary is fundamental rather than methodological.
On a balanced 500-sample test set (Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}), OBD achieves 96\% depth-0 recall but only 14--22\% for depths 2--4; frontier LLMs show a complementary pattern with 69--77\% depth-0 recall and 8--38\% for depths 2--4.
OBD achieves nominally higher overall accuracy (38.0\% vs.\ 33.2\%), but the difference is not statistically significant (McNemar exact test: $p = 0.081$ vs.\ GPT-5.5, $p = 0.069$ vs.\ Claude; bootstrap 95\% CIs include zero: $[-0.4, +10.0]$ and $[0.0, +10.2]$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_llm}): the gap originates entirely from depth-0 identification, while both methods fail comparably at depths $\geq 2$.
This convergence across fundamentally different approaches---supervised statistical classification and zero-shot frontier LLMs---confirms that the saturation is a property of the data rather than a method limitation.

\subsection{The One-Wash Laundering Effect}
\label{sec:one_wash}

The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single round of synthetic generation suffices to render text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled content---a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect that fundamentally limits the granularity of depth-aware corpus curation.
For adversarial robustness, this implies that an adversary need only apply one additional generation pass to make synthetic text indistinguishable from deeper generations, collapsing the depth dimension into a binary signal.

The one-wash effect connects to the model collapse literature: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest retrain-chain generations.
Our prompt-chain results show an analogous pattern at the per-text level, with the first generation step accounting for the dominant share of distributional shift.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage collapse dynamics, $\Kempirical$ could provide a lightweight diagnostic without expensive retraining experiments.

\subsection{Why Graduated Filtering Fails}
\label{sec:negative_graduated}

The failure of graduated strategies to outperform binary filtering (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}) follows directly from the $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary.
Since 2v3 $\auc$ falls below $\theta$ for all configurations (Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci}), depth assignments for $d \geq 2$ approximate random labels.
Graduated weighting ($w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$) then assigns different weights based on these near-random assignments, effectively injecting noise into the importance weights.
This explains the monotonic improvement with $\alpha$ (Table~\ref{tab:tab_alpha_sweep}): as $\alpha$ increases, graduated weighting converges toward a binary threshold, and at $\alpha{=}0.9$ it matches binary-ours on HellaSwag exactly.
DSIR fails for a different reason---its bigram feature hashing captures domain shift but not depth-correlated distributional signatures---underscoring that depth-aware features are necessary for effective curation in recursively contaminated corpora.

\subsection{Representation Dependence of the Boundary}
\label{sec:repr_dependence}

The neural probe results (Table~\ref{tab:neural_probe_crossmodel}) reveal that $\Kempirical$ is representation-dependent: frozen Qwen embeddings yield $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$, while Pythia and OLMo match the 15D boundary at $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 2$.
The Qwen-only elevation is consistent with a \emph{self-familiarity} effect: as an instruction-tuned model, Qwen encodes richer mode-specific artifacts in its hidden states that enable finer depth discrimination when probing its own outputs.
Crucially, the cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) corroborate this interpretation: the generator-specific artifacts that boost Qwen's neural boundary are precisely those that transfer poorly across models (rewrite$\to$continuation: 61--63\% retention vs.\ 80--92\% for continuation-mode pairs).

Cross-scorer validation (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) further illuminates this dependence: when alternative scorers (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B) replace the Qwen self-scorer, feature rankings remain stable ($\rho > 0.90$) but the marginal Qwen-continuation boundary drops from $\Kempirical = 2$ to 1 under both scorers.
The depth signal is text-intrinsic at the level of feature ordering, but absolute discriminability at the boundary is scorer-sensitive---a modulation that is only consequential where the self-scorer margin is already thin (0.15\,pp above $\theta$).
Rewrite mode, with its stronger signal, is scorer-invariant ($\Kempirical = 2$ preserved).

Together, the neural probe and cross-scorer results clarify the practical trade-off for model-free features: the 15D statistical features yield $\Kempirical = 2$ uniformly under self-scoring, but cross-scorer sensitivity reduces the most marginal condition to $\Kempirical = 1$.
The decisive factor is the generation process: both alternative scorers unanimously assign $\Kempirical = 2$ to rewrite-mode text and $\Kempirical = 1$ to continuation-mode text, demonstrating that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the generation operator (rewrite vs.\ continuation) rather than the scoring model.
In open-web settings where the scorer may not match the generator, the continuation-mode cross-scorer boundary defines a conservative lower bound.
Closing the gap between self-scorer and cross-scorer boundaries---and between model-free and neural probe boundaries---remains an open direction.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
5	Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
6	When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
7	This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
8	Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.
9	
10	The gap cuts across three communities.
11	Binary detection methods~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp, zawalski2026codec} produce no depth estimate.
12	The model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} characterizes recursive degradation at the macro level but provides no per-text depth estimation tool.
13	Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} ignore recursive depth.
14	No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.
15	
16	The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
17	We empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations---using 15 statistical features and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
18	We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$.
19	
20	Our primary contribution is a systematic empirical characterization of $\Kempirical$:
21	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

The gap cuts across three communities.
Binary detection methods~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp, zawalski2026codec} produce no depth estimate.
The model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} characterizes recursive degradation at the macro level but provides no per-text depth estimation tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations---using 15 statistical features and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$.

Our primary contribution is a systematic empirical characterization of $\Kempirical$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{$\Kempirical = 2$ at $\theta{=}0.60$} (Cohen's $h{\approx}0.20$) across 4 model-mode configurations (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}) and a decoding strategy ablation on Qwen-rewrite covering 4 strategies (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with all 1v2 CI lower bounds exceeding $\theta$ and all 2v3 CI upper bounds below $\theta$ (permutation $p \leq 0.002$).
  \item \textbf{Cross-model transfer}: 80--92\% accuracy retention across continuation-mode generators; 0v1 $\auc > 0.96$ (range: 0.963--0.991) across all pairs. Cross-scorer validation confirms text-intrinsic feature ordering ($\rho > 0.90$) but scorer-sensitive boundary classification.
  \item \textbf{Feature degradation consistency}: Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ on single-feature rankings across continuation-mode models, with surprisal-variance features dominating.
  \item \textbf{Generation mode}: rewrite yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ ($+$8.4\,pp) but transfers poorly (61--63\% vs.\ 80--92\%).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a secondary contribution, $\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts the strategy ordering in downstream filtering: binary curation at the $\Kempirical$ boundary minimizes degradation most effectively (MMLU $0.5941$ vs.\ base $0.6018$), while graduated ($0.5892$) and surprisal-based ($0.5894$) strategies provide no additional benefit (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).
